text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementNeuroscienceThe Evolutionary Arc From Pigeon Brains to Machine ConsciousnessA conversation with comparative cognition researcher Edward Wasserman about learning and the “edge of chaos”KFBy Kristen French3:00 PM CST on November 5, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleEarlier this year, a bonobo named Kanzi (now deceased) was shown to interact with imaginary grapes and juice, suggesting a capacity for imagination. A review from last year suggested that insects possess subjective experience, citing bumblebees who roll balls without reward and honeybees that opt out of difficult tasks. Other studies suggest some birds and flies have lasting fear memories or that some corvids show causal reasoning. But what does all of this tell us about whether animals possess consciousness?Powered By 10 ShareNextStayComparative cognition researcher Edward Wasserman would say not much. Wasserman, who is a professor at University of Iowa, has been studying pigeon cognition for more than 40 years, particularly the birds’ ability to understand complex concepts. Pigeons are quite intelligent, his findings show, but he says he is highly skeptical of the idea that intelligent behavior can be equated with internal subjective experience. He’s also increasingly interested in what intelligent animal minds can tell us about the nature of intelligent machines. Read more: “Insects and Other Animals May Have Consciousness”Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
